title: Game of Life
topic: Weak areas: redo your mistakes notebook + new
summary: Compute the next generation of Conway's Game of Life in place. Every cell must use the old states of its neighbours, so encode transitions in the cell itself: bit 0 is the current state, bit 1 the next state. After filling every cell's next bit, shift everything right by one.
intuition: Rules: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours lives; a dead cell with exactly 3 becomes alive; everything else dies or stays dead.
`board[r][c] & 1` is still the original state while you're writing bit 1.
A final `>>= 1` turns next states into current states.
pitfalls: Updating cells directly corrupts their neighbours' counts.
Counting the cell itself as a neighbour.
Copying the board works but uses O(m·n) space.

title: 3Sum Closest
topic: Weak areas: redo your mistakes notebook + new
summary: Find three numbers whose sum is closest to the target. Sort, fix the first number, and move two pointers inward: a sum below the target moves the left pointer up, above it moves the right pointer down. Track the closest sum seen.

complexity.note: Sorting plus an O(n) scan per first number.

intuition: Same skeleton as 3Sum, but you keep the best distance instead of exact matches.
An exact match can return immediately.
Moving the pointer toward the target is the only move that can improve the distance.
pitfalls: Initialising `closest` to a huge number and then overflowing on `closest - target`; start with the first triple.

Python.code:
def threeSumClosest(nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
    nums.sort()
    closest = nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2]
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        l, r = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            total = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
            if abs(total - target) < abs(closest - target): closest = total
            if total == target: return total
            if total < target: l += 1
            else: r -= 1
    return closest

title: Integer to English Words
topic: Weak areas: redo your mistakes notebook + new
summary: Spell out a non-negative integer in English. Split it into groups of three digits (ones, thousands, millions, billions). Each group under 1000 is spelled with a small helper that handles hundreds, the teens, and tens; then append the group's scale word.

complexity.note: At most four groups for a 32-bit integer.

intuition: English repeats the same pattern for every three digits, plus a scale word.
Numbers below 20 are irregular, so look them up directly.
Zero itself is a special case.
pitfalls: Extra or trailing spaces; trim at the end.

Python.code:
BELOW_20 = ["", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine", "Ten", "Eleven", "Twelve",
            "Thirteen", "Fourteen", "Fifteen", "Sixteen", "Seventeen", "Eighteen", "Nineteen"]
TENS = ["", "", "Twenty", "Thirty", "Forty", "Fifty", "Sixty", "Seventy", "Eighty", "Ninety"]
SCALES = ["", "Thousand", "Million", "Billion"]


def numberToWords(num: int) -> str:
    if num == 0: return "Zero"
    res, scale = "", 0
    while num > 0:
        chunk = num % 1000
        if chunk: res = three(chunk) + SCALES[scale] + " " + res
        num //= 1000
        scale += 1
    return " ".join(res.split())


def three(n: int) -> str:
    s = ""
    if n >= 100:
        s += BELOW_20[n // 100] + " Hundred "
        n %= 100
    if n >= 20:
        s += TENS[n // 10] + " "
        n %= 10
    if n > 0: s += BELOW_20[n] + " "
    return s
